summary.text: The Kepler space telescope was a NASA telescope launched in 2009 to discover Earth-sized planets orbiting other stars.
Its photometer watched star brightness, and the data were analyzed for periodic dimming caused by planets crossing in front of their stars.
It observed 530,506 stars and discovered 2,662 exoplanets over its lifetime before NASA retired it in 2018.

facts.label: Camera size
facts.value: 94.6 megapixels, largest launched into space then

items.prompt: A planet circles its star in an orbit that never takes it across the star's face as seen from Earth. What would Kepler's method do?

options.label: Detect it by its gravity pulling on the star
Detect it from heat given off by the planet
Miss it, since it only caught planets crossing the star
Detect it by photographing it directly

items.explain: Kepler looked for periodic dimming as planets cross in front of their host star, so only planets whose orbits are seen edge-on could be detected.

items.prompt: Two of Kepler's four pointing wheels failed and could not be fixed. What did NASA do next?

options.label: Approved a modified mission using the working wheels
Sent astronauts to repair the telescope
Stopped planet hunting with it altogether
Switched it to studying only supernovae

items.explain: NASA gave up fixing the two wheels, then approved the K2 extension, which used the remaining two good wheels and thrusters.

options.label: A collision with space debris
A budget cut by NASA
A failed camera sensor
Its reaction control fuel ran out

items.explain: After nine and a half years, the reaction control system fuel was depleted, and NASA announced the retirement.

items.prompt: Kepler's camera was built with a soft focus. Why?

options.label: To give sharp pictures of each planet
To measure brightness precisely rather than sharpness
To keep its sensors from overheating
To cover more sky than a sharp focus

items.explain: The photometer has a soft focus to provide excellent photometry rather than sharp images.

items.prompt: Besides planets, what else did Kepler's half-hourly brightness measurements help scientists study?

options.label: Supernovae
Comet tails
Solar flares
Black hole jets

items.explain: Measurements were collected every half-hour, so the light curves were especially useful for studying supernovae.

items.prompt: Kepler's team needed more than the planned three and a half years. What was the reason?

options.label: The telescope was launched late
The data were noisier than expected
The telescope moved too slowly
The funding had to be repaid

items.explain: Greater-than-expected noise in the data, from both the stars and the spacecraft, meant additional time was needed.

paragraphs.heading: What Kepler was
paragraphs.text: Kepler was a space telescope that NASA launched in 2009 to look for Earth-sized planets around other stars. It belonged to NASA's Discovery Program, a line of relatively low-cost science missions. It was named after the astronomer Johannes Kepler, who, oddly enough, was sure that no other stars had planets. Rather than circling Earth, the spacecraft went around the Sun, trailing behind Earth.

paragraphs.heading: How it hunted planets
paragraphs.text: Its only science instrument was a photometer, which kept measuring the brightness of about 150,000 stars in one fixed patch of sky. The aim was to find Earth-size planets in or close to habitable zones, and to judge what share of the Milky Way's billions of stars host such worlds. Back on Earth, scientists searched the data for regular dips in brightness caused by a planet passing in front of its star. This only works when we see the planet's orbit edge-on. The photometer was kept slightly out of focus on purpose, because precise brightness readings mattered more than sharp pictures.

paragraphs.heading: The hardware
paragraphs.text: Kepler had a mass of 1,039 kilograms. Its camera sent light from a 0.95-meter front lens onto a 1.4-meter mirror, which at launch was the biggest mirror on any telescope beyond Earth orbit. Its view covered 115 square degrees of sky, about the size of your fist held out at arm's length. The light fell on forty-two CCD chips with 94.6 megapixels in all, at the time the largest camera system sent into space.

paragraphs.heading: Broken wheels and a second life
paragraphs.text: The mission was planned to last three and a half years, but the data were noisier than expected, from both the stars and the spacecraft, so more time was needed. In July 2012 one of the four reaction wheels that pointed the spacecraft stopped turning. In May 2013 a second one failed, which halted science data collection, and in August NASA gave up trying to fix them. A new plan called K2, or Second Light, was reported that November: it would use the damaged telescope to look for habitable planets around smaller, dimmer red dwarfs. NASA approved it in May 2014.

paragraphs.heading: What it found
paragraphs.text: By January 2015, Kepler and follow-up observations had turned up 1,013 confirmed planets in about 440 star systems. That month NASA announced Kepler's 1,000th confirmed planet; four of the newly confirmed ones orbited in their stars' habitable zones, and three of those (Kepler-438b, Kepler-442b and Kepler-452b) are close to Earth in size and probably rocky. In May 2016 NASA verified 1,284 more Kepler planets at once, the largest single haul of planets to date. Using Kepler data, astronomers estimated in 2013 that the Milky Way might hold up to 40 billion rocky Earth-size planets in habitable zones, around both red dwarfs and stars like the Sun, with 11 billion of them around Sun-like stars.

paragraphs.heading: The end of the mission
paragraphs.text: After nine and a half years, Kepler used up the fuel for its reaction control system. NASA announced its retirement on October 30, 2018, and it was shut down that same day. Over its life it observed 530,506 stars and discovered 2,662 planets. Because it took measurements every half hour, its data also helped scientists study supernovae. A newer NASA mission, TESS, launched in 2018, carries the planet search on.
